title: Requirements & Lifecycle
subtitle: what to build, in which phase

beats.narration: Before any platform decision comes the question of where requirements come from. A business problem — help support agents answer faster — is not a requirement yet. This section turns it into requirements a deployment decision can be defended against, then places all of this module's work on one lifecycle.

elements.text: "answer faster" is not a requirement — yet

goal: requirements a decision
can be DEFENDED against

beats.narration: A functional requirement names what the system must do, stated with enough detail to check. From help agents answer faster, you derive: classify each ticket into one of four queues. Draft a reply citing the relevant policy. Never auto-send without human approval. Each one is a checkable statement of behavior — a line in an eval, a criterion at review. If it can't be checked, it can't be designed against.

beats.narration: Infrastructure requirements are the constraints the deployment must satisfy — and most are never stated. You derive them by asking what the business problem implies. Latency: how fast, measured where the user is. Scale: how many requests, at what peak. Residency: where the data must be processed, and under which regulation. Identity: who acts, under what credentials, with what audit. These four most often decide the platform, and they're cheapest to capture before a platform gets chosen for other reasons. Then write the record down — behaviors, constraints, and the regulation each comes from — because the decision will be reviewed by people who didn't gather them.

items.text: latency — how fast, where the user is
scale — how many, at what peak

beats.narration: Second half: the systems lifecycle, the arc all of this module's work sits on. Requirements, design, build, test, deploy, operate, iterate — the same phases the earlier modules taught one at a time. The connection is the gates. You don't move from design to build until the platform satisfies the residency requirement. You don't promote a deployment until the new version clears the eval against the pinned baseline. Placing work in its phase, and refusing to skip a gate, is what keeps the application reviewable. A one-off experiment may collapse phases. A regulated deployment cannot.

elements.code:
requirements → design → build → test
      → deploy → operate → iterate ↺

elements.text:
the GATES between phases
= where control lives

design→build: residency satisfied first
deploy→prod: eval beats the baseline first
experiments collapse phases · regulated builds don't

beats.narration: The reflex: derive the constraints before anyone names a platform, and let every phase change pass its gate. Two checkpoints follow — extract requirements from a bank scenario, and place activities on the lifecycle. One debrief covers both. Then: deployment and versioning.

elements.text:
constraints before platforms ·
no phase change skips its gate
